extracted.intended_audience: American statesmen, legislators, and educated readers interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and descriptive principles for designing and evaluating republican constitutions (balance of powers, magistracy, assemblies, election methods, law enforcement, and representation) illustrated by historical examples (Geneva, Venice, England, Netherlands, America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of three powers for balance
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be, in the nature of things, no balance without three powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues repeatedly that a durable political balance requires three orders/powers (e.g., a first magistrate, an aristocracy, and the people or their representation). Single or two-fold arrangements tend to be unstable: aristocracy will outwit assemblies, magistrates may usurp, and assemblies alone cannot properly check aristocratic domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating all authority in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing all things in one assembly, or collecting all authority into one center, leads magistrates to 'do as they please' and undermines accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When magistrates and people meet in one assembly the former will eventually dominate; annual reviews become a farce, councils become perpetual and independent of the people. Example: Geneva's general assembly devolving power to permanent councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a first magistrate to check powerful families
rubrics_metrics.description: A power above them in a first magistrate is necessary to control invincible attachment of people to a few families and the families' attempts to grasp authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites the danger that, without a strong first magistrate, powerful families will concentrate authority. The first magistrate serves as a counterweight to family oligarchies and should have sufficient authority to prevent capture of the state by factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix rights and attributes of orders by law
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights and attributes of all the orders of the state are fixed by the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codifying the positions and powers of the orders (magistracy, councils, citizens) in law constrains arbitrary alteration and provides legal clarity. Geneva's constitutionality of orders is given as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constitutional, peaceful means to change rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the people a legal, constitutional, and peaceable mode of changing these rulers; this avoids continual violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises procedures that allow removal/replacement of rulers by legal means (elections, reviews) as essential to prevent violent uprisings; contrasted with states where lack of such mechanisms precipitated assassination, revolt, or tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctual execution of the laws is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A punctual execution of the laws is, no doubt, essential to the existence of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict, impartial enforcement (even severe punishments) is described as a practical means by which states (Venice example) restrained princes, nobles, and people from violating orders; tribunals like the state inquisition are cited as mechanisms that preserved order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance courts and councils against one another (mutual checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great care is taken... to balance one court against another, and render their powers mutual checks to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venice's institutional architecture — multiple colleges, senates, councils, and rotating officers — is given as exemplifying careful internal checks so no single body or office becomes dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use layered/complex election procedures to limit faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt complex, multi-stage ballot procedures to choose magistrates in order to avoid factional control and undue influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'famous ballot of Venice' (multiple rounds of drawing gilt/white balls, successive elector reductions) is described as a deliberate design to reduce partisan capture and ensure impartial selection of the doge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hereditary magistracy and hereditary legislative transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make first magistrates hereditary nor make senators hereditary; hereditary offices weaken constitutional balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises republican practice (America) of avoiding hereditary rulers and criticises attempts to make councils or magistracies hereditary (Venice example), arguing hereditary transmission concentrates power and defeats accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep offices open to merit rather than exclusive family privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices should be open to all men of merit; avoid exclusive preferences of families or nobles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United Provinces (Netherlands) example: by law offices were open to merit, avoiding exclusive noble privilege. Opening offices by merit reduces aristocratic dominance and encourages talent-based governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure equitable representation in representative assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people are not equitably represented in the house of commons, this is a departure in practice from the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable representation is necessary for the practical functioning of balance. Lack of fair representation distorts the balance of powers and may prompt corrective measures or destabilizing alliances between crown and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the executive with a negative (veto) as a balancing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The giving of a negative upon the legislature to the executive power (a veto) is an important element of balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes the Americans did not adopt an executive negative at the time and considers that an incompleteness in their system of checks; a veto is presented as a stabilizing counterweight between branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful rotation/term limits and effective accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual reviews and elections must be substantive and meaningful; otherwise they become a farce and enable permanent, independent councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where annual reviews were perfunctory only for egregious faults were officials excluded — leading to de facto perpetual magistracies. Genuine rotation and enforceable accountability are necessary to prevent oligarchic entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct intermediary bodies to distribute cognizance of affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave cognizance of details to subordinate officers or councils (e.g., syndics, assessors) rather than concentrating all business in a general assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the time of the Reformation Geneva left details to four syndics; delegation helps manage multiplicity of affairs and binds citizens to the commonwealth by creating durable administrative ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to balance aristocracy by democracy alone without a third power
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing an aristocratical by a democratical assembly, without the aid of a third power, is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that placing only two orders in opposition will not yield stable checks — a third, distinct power or order is required to mediate and maintain equilibrium (historical failures in Geneva and elsewhere are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design severe, impartial tribunals to deter conspiracies and preserve order
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunals exercising rigorous impartiality and severe penalties (e.g., state inquisitors) are used to keep doge, nobility, and people in awe and restrain violations of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venice's state inquisition and 'lions' mouths' are given as extreme examples where harsh, often secretive procedures (e.g., close confinement, execution by plurality vote, power to search ducal apartments) served to deter conspiracies and preserve the aristocratic republic's longevity.
